chunks: "Each phase has its own inductor and FETs, and all the inductor currents flow into the same output node, so by KCL the output current is the sum of the phase currents.
A single stage can only carry so much, limited by the FETs' conduction loss and temperature, by the inductor's saturation and heating current, and by the package and the copper.
With four phases each stage only has to carry a quarter of the load, so a 60 amp load becomes four 15 amp stages, which are parts that are easy to buy and cool.
In practice you don't get exactly N times the single-stage rating. The currents are never perfectly equal, so the most heavily loaded phase hits its limit first.
If the sense error and mismatch are 5 percent, the usable total is about N times the phase limit divided by 1. 05.
You also have to look at the peak current: the DC current plus half the ripple has to stay below the inductor's saturation current.
And you leave margin for temperature, and for what happens if one phase fails and the others pick up its share.
So a 4-phase design built from 25 amp derated stages is good for about 95 amps, and I would rate the system for somewhat less than that."
